# Notes on Matthew 20

**Gaps to know about first.** Enduring Word's page (David Guzik) cut off partway through vv. 17–19. Ellicott's page cut off at v. 17. Because of that, my notes on vv. 24–27 and 31–34 are thin. I didn't find anything from bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, oca.org, the Lutheran sites or the Pentecostal sites, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those sections are left out rather than filled from memory.

## The parable of the workers (vv. 1–16)

**v. 1**
- **Context:** Guzik says the parable answers Peter's question in 19:27, "what shall we have?" He describes the marketplace as the place where day laborers waited to be hired. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- **The chapter break:** Ellicott thinks it was badly placed, because it cuts the parable off from the rich young ruler story that prompted it. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- **What the figures stand for:**
  - Ellicott: the householder is Christ, and the vineyard is mainly Israel (as in Isaiah 5). The early-morning workers are the first disciples. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
  - Gill (Reformed Baptist): the vineyard may be the church, separated from the world "by electing, redeeming, and calling grace". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/20-1.htm
  - Matthew Henry: the church is God's vineyard, which He planted, waters and fences. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_020.cfm
- **Spurgeon:** this was no ordinary employer. He "considered the laborers rather than himself." https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew-20-commentary-spurgeon

**v. 2**
- Guzik: a denarius was the normal day's wage, and this was a completely ordinary deal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- Ellicott: it was a fair and adequate wage. In the parable's meaning, the denarius stands for the kingdom, or eternal life. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm

**vv. 3–5**
- **The hours:** Guzik counts from 6 a.m.: the third hour is about 9 a.m., the sixth is noon, and the eleventh is about 5 p.m. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- **The urgency:** Guzik quotes Barclay that the grape harvest was a race against the coming rains. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- **v. 4, "whatever is right":** Ellicott notes the later workers had no contract and simply trusted the owner. His lesson: a little work done in trust is better than a lot done in a hireling's spirit. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm

**vv. 6–7**
- Ellicott: the last workers had never turned down an earlier call, and they came at once, in faith. He also wonders whether the first workers were working less eagerly than they might have. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- Spurgeon (via Guzik) turns it into a question for the reader: why is any of us standing idle toward God? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: paying wages the same evening kept the Mosaic law (Deuteronomy 24:15). Paying the last first acts out "the last shall be first." https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- Guzik: the order mattered. Paying the last first is what gave the first workers time to expect more. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/

**vv. 9–10**
- Ellicott: the latecomers weren't idle by their own fault, so they got a full wage. The pay was based on quality, not quantity: no true worker gets less than eternal life, and no long life of work can claim more. He thinks the disciples should have seen their own wish for special rank in the first workers. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm

**vv. 11–12**
- Ellicott: the Greek tense for "grumble" points to repeated, drawn-out complaining. The "scorching heat" may be the hot wind that follows sunrise. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- Matthew Henry applies it to Gentiles, who were newly called in and given as much of the kingdom's privileges as the Jews who had long labored. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Mat/Mat_020.cfm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: when Jesus says "friend," it always carries a note of rebuke. He uses it for the guest without a wedding garment and for Judas. He adds that no true Christian would resent the thief on the cross his place in Paradise. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- Guzik: the owner broke no promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/

**v. 14**
- Guzik: the owner gives no reason beyond "I want to." The reason for his generosity lies in him, not in the people who receive it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- Ellicott admits it is hard to say what the dismissal stands for spiritually. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm

**v. 15**
- **"Envious" (literally "evil eye"):** both Guzik (citing Carson and Clarke) and Ellicott explain the "evil eye" as a Jewish idiom for jealousy or envy. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): eternal life is God's free gift, so He may give it in whatever proportions, at whatever times and on whatever conditions He pleases. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/matthew-20.html

**v. 16**
- **Main reading:** Guzik says the parable is best read as being about grace and reward. God is never less than fair, but may be more than fair. He mentions, but doesn't prefer, two other readings: stages of a person's life, or stages of salvation history. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- **Degrees of reward:** Ellicott says the verse doesn't teach that everyone's blessedness is equal. There will be "first" and "last," but this depends on the worker's character, not on how long he served. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- **Missing words (why the BSB has no "many are called, but few chosen"):** Ellicott notes that the better manuscripts leave the line out here. He makes the Jew/Gentile reading secondary to the parable's main point. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm

## Where traditions differ on the parable

- **Chrysostom (a Church Father honored by both Orthodox and Catholics):**
  - The vineyard is God's commandments, the working day is this present life, and the hours are the different ages at which people come to God.
  - God called everyone, and "the difference was made by the disposition of them that were called."
  - https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200164.htm
- **Hawker (Reformed/Calvinist):** the equal wage shows "free and sovereign grace." No merit in anyone makes "the smallest claim to favor." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/matthew-20.html
- **The contrast:** Chrysostom puts the difference in timing down to how people respond. Gill and Hawker stress electing, sovereign grace. That is an Arminian/Calvinist difference, though I didn't find a source that sets the two side by side.

## The third prediction of the Passion (vv. 17–19)

- **v. 17:** Ellicott places the raising of Lazarus and the stay at Ephraim (John 10–11) between vv. 16 and 17. He draws on Mark to show that Jesus walked ahead alone, and the disciples were amazed and afraid. https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/20.htm
- **v. 18:** Guzik says the disciples don't seem to have really taken in the warning because they were expecting a political kingdom. He quotes Spurgeon that Judas heard this prediction of betrayal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- **v. 19:** Guzik notes how specific the prediction is, covering things Jesus had no obvious control over. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/

## The request of James and John (vv. 20–23)

**v. 20**
- Barnes: the mother was probably Salome. Mark says the sons asked, so they likely asked through her. She may have been ambitious for them. "Knelt" means paying respect. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html

**v. 21**
- Barnes: they still expected an earthly kingdom. Sitting at a king's right and left was the highest honor. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html

**v. 22**
- Barnes: in Scripture the "cup" often means suffering or punishment, like the bitter cup God gave His Son. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html
- Chrysostom: Jesus answers their talk of crowns with talk of struggles and labors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/matthew/20.htm

**v. 23, "You will indeed drink My cup":**
- Barnes and Haydock (Catholic): this came true. James was martyred (Acts 12:2). John was exiled to Patmos, and Haydock adds the tradition that he was put into boiling oil at Rome. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-20.html

**v. 23, "not Mine to grant"** (the most debated phrase in the chapter):
- **Wording:** Barnes, Clarke and Maclaren all say the KJV's added words ("it shall be given to them") distort the sense. Barnes's reading: Jesus does give the rewards, but only to those the Father has prepared them for.
  - Barnes: https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-23.html
  - Clarke: https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/matthew-20.html
  - Maclaren: https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/matthew/nearest-to-christ.cfm
- **Ellicott:** Jesus gives them, but in line with His Father's will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/20-23.htm
- **Catholic (Haydock):** the Arians used these words against Christ's divinity. Augustine answered that they are true of Christ as man. Haydock's "easier answer" is that the seats weren't His to give to them while they were so proud. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/matthew-20.html
- **Aquinas's Golden Chain (quoting Augustine and Remigius):** Christ answers "in His character of servant," since whatever the Father prepares, the Son also prepares. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcc/matthew-20.html
- **Guzik:** the phrase shows Christ's remarkable submission to His Father. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-20/
- **Hawker (Reformed):** he reads it as covenant election. It is for those the Father gave to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pmc/matthew-20.html

## Greatness through service (vv. 24–28)

**v. 24**
- Barnes: the ten were angry at the two brothers' request and ambition, not at what Jesus said. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html
- Bridgeway: James and John may have had Peter especially in mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html

**vv. 25–27**
- Barnes: Christ's kingdom is set up differently from the nations, where rulers raise their favorites. "Servant" in v. 26 is the Greek word for deacon. Ministers are servants, so they must not lord it over God's people. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html

**v. 28, Jesus' example:** Calvin and Barnes both connect this to Philippians 2:7, Christ taking "the form of a servant." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html

**v. 28, "ransom":**
- Ellicott: the word means a price paid for release. He points to Old Testament uses in the Greek translation (Exodus 21:30; Leviticus 25:50). https://biblehub.com/matthew/20-28.htm
- Barnes: Christ died in sinners' place. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html
- Ligonier: some in the early church thought the ransom was paid to the devil. That view has been rejected by the vast majority of Christian thinkers. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/atonement-as-ransom

**v. 28, "for many" — where Protestants differ:**
- **Gill (Calvinist Baptist):** the ransom was paid for "his people," in their room and stead. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/asv/matthew/20-28.html
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** he preached his sermon "Particular Redemption" on this text. https://biblehub.com/study/matthew/20-28.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** he takes the opposite line from Gill here. "Many" doesn't mean a fixed number. Christ is contrasting Himself with everyone else, the way Romans 5:15 embraces "the whole human race." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** Christ certainly died for all, citing 1 Timothy 2:6. https://biblehub.com/matthew/20-28.htm
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian):** he also cites 1 Timothy 2:6, "a ransom for all." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html
- **Clarke (Methodist):** he reads it as one ransom instead of the many sacrifices required by the Jewish law. He also notes a long extra passage about seating at feasts in Codex Bezae and some old versions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html

**v. 28, Protestant vs. Catholic:** Calvin says this one word overturns "the idle talk of the Papists" about acts of satisfaction for sin. Note this is Calvin's own polemic, not a Catholic source. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-28.html

## The two blind men near Jericho (vv. 29–34)

**vv. 29–30, one man or two?** Mark and Luke mention one blind man, Matthew two. Luke also says Jesus was entering Jericho, not leaving.
- Gill, Barnes and Clarke: Mark and Luke never say there was *only* one. They name Bartimaeus because he was well known. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-30.html
- Calvin: perhaps one man cried out first and the second followed his example. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-30.html
- GotQuestions: there were two Jerichos at the time, the old mound and the inhabited city. Jesus could have been leaving one and entering the other. https://www.gotquestions.org/one-two-blind-men.html
- Catholic Answers agrees that mentioning one doesn't deny that there were two. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-ballad-of-blind-bartimaeus

**v. 30, "Son of David":** Constable says the title expressed their belief that Jesus was the Messiah. He suggests Matthew may name both men to give two witnesses for his Jewish readers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-30.html

**vv. 31–34**
- Barclay: they asked boldly, not for money but for sight, and afterwards they followed Jesus out of gratitude. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-30.html
- Barnes: the blind men picture the sinner, who is blinded by sin and must call on Jesus to open his eyes. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/20-29.html
